In contrast, Reviewer 4 (disruptive-thinking lens) identifies 'high disruptive potential' due to the architectural simplification of direct SQL generation bypassing logical forms, and the novel integrated feedback loop for rapid, 'from scratch' deployment. This represents a controlled disagreement on the *degree* and *type* of innovation, rather than a factual contradiction.
uncertainty_snapshot: Qualitative claims such as 'rapidly and easily,' 'high-quality,' and 'minimal intervention' (C1) lack precise quantitative metrics or baselines for rigorous interpretation, making their 'high-quality' aspect relative.

The claim of 'comparable accuracy' on benchmark datasets (C2) is nuanced, as the paper explicitly notes 'slightly lower accuracy than the best non-SQL results' compared to some prior work, and comparisons are complicated by different evaluation metrics and data conversions.

The claim of learning 'from scratch' (C3) is qualified by the initial training on synthetically generated data from schema templates and paraphrases, meaning the model is not initialized with zero domain-specific knowledge.

The claim that data augmentation 'consistently improves performance' (C4) is overstated for schema templates, as they 'does not improve performance in the fully supervised setting,' their 'advantage is reduced as more labeled data is obtained,' and they 'did not improve accuracy on ATIS.'

The claim that SQL's popularity makes crowd-sourced annotations 'easier and cheaper' than logical forms (C6) is a plausible hypothesis but remains an unverified assumption within the paper's scope, explicitly noted as 'an exploration we leave to future work' without empirical evidence or cost analysis.

The terms 'arbitrary SQL queries' and 'full expressivity' (C7) are strong and not fully quantified; while the model avoids limitations of some rule-based systems, the practical limits of 'arbitrary' within NLIDB contexts are not exhaustively demonstrated.

The claim that the approach is 'language-agnostic and portable to other query languages' (C9) is a forward-looking statement lacking empirical validation within the paper, as specific components are tailored to SQL.

The long-term impact of acknowledged user feedback errors (6.1% correct marked wrong, 6.3% incorrect marked correct) (A2) on model stability or the rate of improvement is not fully explored, despite being stated as 'sufficient.'

The finding that more frequent deployments reduce annotation effort (C8) is based on simulated interactive learning experiments on GEO880, which may not fully reflect the dynamics of a live online system with imperfect user input.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Large-scale Semantic Parsing without Question-Answer Pairs Siva Reddy, Mirella Lapata, Mark Steedman School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh 10 Crichton Street, Edinburgh EH8 9AB siva.reddy@ed.ac.uk, mlap@inf.ed.ac.uk, steedman@inf.ed.ac.uk Abstract In this paper we introduce a novel semantic parsing approach to query Freebase in natu- ral language without requiring manual anno- tations or question-answer pairs. Our key in- sight is to represent natural language via se- mantic graphs whose topology shares many commonalities with Freebase. Given this rep- resentation, we conceptualize semantic pars- ing as a graph matching problem. Our model converts sentences to semantic graphs using CCG and subsequently grounds them to Free- base guided by denotations as a form of weak supervision. Evaluation experiments on a sub- set of the F REE 917 and W EBQUESTIONS benchmark datasets show our semantic parser improves over the state of the art. 1 Introduction Querying a database to retrieve an answer, telling a robot to perform an action, or teaching a com- puter to play a game are tasks requiring communi- cation with machines in a language interpretable by them. Semantic parsing addresses the speciﬁc task of learning to map natural language (NL) to machine interpretable formal meaning representations. Tra- ditionally, sentences are converted into logical form grounded in the symbols of some ﬁxed ontology or relational database. Approaches for learning semantic parsers

In this paper, we show it can be used within a grounded CCG semantic parsing approach that learns a joint model of mean- ing and context for interpreting and executing natural language instructions, using various types of weak supervision. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
